1:1: The word Nun is the name of a man, Joshua’s father.
1:2: The Lord is using the expression arise to tell Joshua to take action and lead the Israelites across the Jordan River to begin the conquest of Canaan. He is not telling him to get out of bed or stand up from a seated position.
As the Introduction to Joshua discusses, here and in many places throughout the book, sons means “descendants,” so the phrase sons of is describing a people group.
1:3: The Lord is using part of each of the Israelites, the sole of your foot, to represent the people of Israel themselves.
1:4: The phrase the Great River is another name used for the Euphrates River.
The phrase the Great Sea is another name for the “Mediterranean Sea.”
The Lord is using the going of the sun, that is, the sunset, by association to mean “the west,” since the sun sets in the west.
1:5: In this context the phrase to your face either means “in front of you,” with face meaning by association the area in front of Joshua, or “against you,” with part of Joshua, his face, representing all of him.
The phrases I will not abandon you and I will not leave you mean the same thing. The Lord says the same thing twice, in slightly different ways, to emphasize to Joshua that he will be with him.
1:6: The phrases Be strong and be courageous mean similar things. The Lord is using the two terms together for emphasis.
Here, fathers means “ancestors” and refers specifically to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
1:7: These are the same two phrases that occurred in the previous verse, except the word very is added here for increased emphasis.

The Lord is speaking as if the law that Moses … commanded were literally a road that Joshua was walking on and as if Joshua might turn aside from it and walk on a different path. He means that Joshua must not stop living in the manner in which God commanded in the law.
The Lord is speaking of two things in order to mean those things and everything in between them. Continuing the image of the road, he means that Joshua should not go off the road in any direction.
1:8: The Lord is using the phrase shall not depart from your mouth by association to mean that Joshua must continually read the Book of the Law, since people at this time read aloud, even when reading alone, so Joshua would use his mouth to form the words as he read. (However, this is not a command to read only alone. It envisions that Joshua might at times read the law aloud to the people of Israel.)
The Lord is using the two phrases together for emphasis.

The Lord is speaking of Joshua’s ways as if they were a living thing that Joshua could make … prosperous. The Lord is speaking of Joshua’s actions as if they were ways or roads that he was walking on.
1:9: The Lord is using the question form for emphasis.
The phrases Do not be terrified and do not be dismayed mean similar things. The Lord combines them to emphasize that Joshua must not fear.
1:11: Joshua was counting the current day as day one. This was the way that Jewish people counted days.
1:13: Joshua did not think that the people from these three tribes had forgotten what Moses had instructed them. Rather, he is using the word Remember to cause them to pay attention to what he is going to say next.
Here, word represents what Moses had said to Joshua using words.
The phrase giving rest is an idiom that refers to living peacefully and settling down in the land after Israel defeats its enemies.
1:14: Here, the word translated as livestock refers to cows, sheep, and goats.
Joshua is describing this land from the perspective of the land that the Lord originally promised to the Israelites west of the Jordan.
See the Introduction to Joshua for a discussion of the phrase “to the face of.”
Here, the word brothers means “fellow Israelites” and refers to the Israelites from the other tribes of Israel.
The phrase the warriors of valor refers to the men who were of fighting age, over 20 years old.
1:15: The phrase gives rest refers to living peacefully and settling down in the land after Israel defeated its enemies. It has the same meaning as the phrase “giving rest” in Joshua 1:13.
1:18: כָּל־אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר־יַמְרֶה אֶת־פִּיךָ וְלֹא־יִשְׁמַע אֶת־דְּבָרֶיךָ לְכֹל אֲשֶׁר־תְּצַוֶּנּוּ יוּמָת

These two phrases mean basically the same thing and emphasize that any form of disobedience will be punished. The phrase disobeys your mouth and the phrase will not hear your words mean basically the same thing. The speakers are saying the same thing twice, in slightly different ways, to emphasize that they will put to death anyone who disobeys what Joshua commands.
The speakers are using the words mouth and words and associating them with the instructions or commands that Joshua would speak with his mouth using words.
2:1: This is the name of a place on the east side of the Jordan River. It means “acacia trees.”
2:2: The person addressing the king is speaking as if he wants him to look at something, but he is actually using the term Behold to focus attention on what he is about to say.
2:6: The author is providing this background information to explain how Rahab had hidden the men, as described in Joshua 2:4.
The roof was flat and strong, so people could walk around on it.
The word flax refers to a plant that is grown for its fibers, which are used in making cloth. It has tall, slender stalks that can be tied into bundles.
2:7: The word fords describes places where a river or other body of water is shallow enough for people to get to the other side by walking through it.
2:9: Here, the word you is plural and refers to all the Israelite people.
Rahab is speaking as if dread or fear of the Israelites had actually fallen on the people of Jericho and Canaan.
Rahab is speaking as if the people of Jericho and Canaan had actually melted in front of or in the presence of the Israelites. The implication is that they will not be able to resist the Israelites.
2:10: See the discussion in the Introduction to Joshua of the term that is here translated as devoted. In this context, the term refers to complete destruction.
2:11: Rahab is using one part of a person, his spirit, to mean all of him in the act of resisting or not.
Rahab is using the two major components of creation to mean all of creation itself.
2:12: Rahab is not using the expression the house of my father to refer to the building in which her father lives. As the next verse indicates, the expression means her extended family, which included her parents, her siblings, and their spouses and children.
2:13: Rahab is speaking as if death itself were threatening the lives of her family so that the spies needed to deliver or rescue them from it. She is using death to represent the Israelite army, which was about to enter Canaan and kill its inhabitants.
2:14: This is an oath formula in which the two spies are promising to give their lives (allow themselves to be killed) if they do not keep their promise and spare the lives of Rahab and her family when the Israelites conquer Jericho and kill its inhabitants.
The terms kindness and faithfulness mean similar things. The spies are using the two terms together for emphasis.
2:15: The author is describing a particular event before describing other events that preceded it. This actually occurred after Rahab spoke her final words to the spies in Joshua 2:21.
כִּי בֵיתָהּ בְּקִיר הַחוֹמָה וּבַחוֹמָה הִיא יוֹשָׁבֶת

The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens in the story. Because Rahab’s house was built into the city wall, she was able to let the spies out a window and lower them down to the ground outside the city wall. That way they were able to escape from the city even though the gates had been shut.
2:17: נְקִיִּם אֲנַחְנוּ מִשְּׁבֻעָתֵךְ הַזֶּה אֲשֶׁר הִשְׁבַּעְתָּנוּ

The spies are implicitly introducing the conditions that Rahab and her family must meet in order for their lives to be spared. If they do not meet these conditions, then the spies will be innocent, that is, not guilty of breaking their oath, if Rahab and her family are killed.
2:18: The spies are using a common expression that means that they were about to do something.
The word scarlet describes a bright red color.
2:19: The spies are using one part of Rahab’s house, its doors, to mean all it.
The spies are using a common expression that means that someone is morally and legally responsible for something.
The spies are using the expression a hand shall be upon to mean that someone would be injured or harmed.
2:21: This expression indicates that Rahab agreed to the men’s terms of the oath.
Rahab is using the term words by association to mean what the spies said by using words.
2:23: The author is speaking of what the spies saw and experienced as they investigated Jericho as if those were living things that could have found them.
2:24: In this expression, having something in one’s hand represents, by association, possessing it.
3:4: The word cubit means a measurement equaling the distance from the elbow to the end of the middle finger tip.
3:6: See the Introduction to Joshua for a discussion of the phrase “to the face of.”
3:9: Joshua is using the term words to represent what the Lord is about to say by using words.
3:12: Joshua is using a common expression to indicate individuals representing groups to which they belong.
3:15: וְהַיַּרְדֵּן מָלֵא עַל־כָּל־גְּדוֹתָיו כֹּל יְמֵי קָצִיר

The author is providing background information to help readers appreciate how great a miracle the Lord did on this occasion. The implication is that the Israelites crossed the Jordan River during the days of the harvest, so the Lord stopped its waters even when they were overflowing its banks.
The author is using the term days to refer to a specific time.
3:16: The words the sea of Arabah and Sea of Salt are both names for what is now known as “the Dead Sea.”
4:3: Joshua is using one part of the priests, their feet, to mean all of them in the act of standing in the Jordan riverbed.
4:5: See the Introduction to Joshua for a discussion of the phrase “to the face of.”
4:6: Joshua is speaking as if the children of this generation of Israelites would ask about the stones on the day after this event, tomorrow.
The children of these Israelites would be using a common expression to ask about the significance of the stones for their parents.
4:7: See the discussion of this sentence in the introduction to this chapter.
Joshua means implicitly that the priests carried the Box of the Covenant of the Lord over the Jordan River. He is not saying that it crossed over on its own.
4:9: As the Introduction to Joshua discusses, the author is using the term day by association to refer to a specific time, the time when he was writing this book. He means that the 12 stones were still in the middle of the Jordan at the time he wrote this account of them.
4:10: This phrase expresses a single idea by using two words connected with and. The word hurried tells in what way the people crossed over.
4:11: This phrase expresses a single idea by using two words connected with and. The phrase the priests indicates how the Box of the Lord crossed the Jordan River.
4:14: The author is using the term days to refer to a specific time, the lifetime of Moses.
4:19: The first month of the Hebrew calendar is named Aviv. The ‘first month’ was the month of Aviv. That was in the spring of the year. It corresponds to March and April on Western calendars.
4:24: Here, hand represents the capability and power of a person.
Joshua is using the term days by association to mean “time,” since time is made up of days.
5:2: The word flint describes a type of hard stone known for having sharp edges.

This does not mean that these men had already been circumcised once and that the Lord wanted Joshua to circumcise each of them for a second time. Rather, as Joshua 5:4 explains, the previous generation of male Israelites had been circumcised, but they had died in the wilderness; the current generation of Israelite males had not yet been circumcised.
5:3: There were over 600,000 males, so the author is using Joshua, who was in charge of this task, to represent the many people who were necessarily involved.

Gibeath Haaraloth is the name that the Israelites gave to the place where they held this second general circumcision ceremony. The name commemorates the Israelites rededicating themselves to the Lord.
5:6: The author seems to be speaking as if these men of war were a nation of their own. In this language and culture, people sometimes used the term “nation” to mean “army,” as in Joel 1:6, for example.
The author is using the voice of the Lord by association to mean the things that the Lord commanded by using his voice.
The Lord spoke of the land being good for animals and plants as if the milk and honey from those animals and plants were actually flowing through the land.
5:8: The author is using the term nation as in Joshua 5:6, to refer specifically to the Israelite males.
5:9: The Lord is speaking as if he had actually rolled away the disgrace of Egypt from the Israelites.
5:13: The author is using a common expression to mean that Joshua looked some distance away, since he lifted up his eyes in order to do this, and he had to walk over to the man whom he saw.
The author is using the term behold to focus the reader’s attention on what Joshua saw standing in front of him.
5:14: The phrase fell on his face to the earth means that Joshua intentionally got down on his knees and touched the ground with his face. In that culture, this action was a way that a person showed great respect and reverence for someone else.
5:15: Joshua removing his sandal was a symbolic action by which he showed great respect and reverence toward someone superior and acknowledged his willingness to obey him.
6:1: The author is providing background information that will help readers understand what happens next in the story.

The phrases Now Jericho was shutting and was being shut up and There was no going out and there was no coming in mean basically the same thing. The author is using them together for emphasis. See the further discussion in the introduction to this chapter.
6:2: The Lord is speaking as if he wants Joshua to See or look at something. He is actually using the term to focus Joshua’s attention on what he is about to say.
Here, hand represents by association the control or power that a person would have over something.
6:3: The context implies that they were to walk around the city one time each day.
6:5: In this context, the phrase the people refers to the Israelite soldiers.
Here, the phrase go up refers to climbing up over the collapsed pieces of the walls to get into the city.
The Lord is using a common expression to mean that each of the soldiers in the army that is encircling the city should rush into the part of it that is directly in front of him.
6:7: The phrase Pass over is a common expression that indicates walking or moving forward.
6:8: As the last sentence in this verse makes clear, the author is using the name The Lord by association to mean the Box of the Covenant of the Lord, since it represents the Lord’s presence with the people of Israel.
The author does not mean that the Box of the Covenant of the Lord was going by itself. Priests were carrying it.
6:9: Here again, it is implied that priests were carrying the Box.
6:10: As in Joshua 6:5, the phrase the people refers to the Israelite soldiers.
לֹא תָרִיעוּ וְלֹא־תַשְׁמִיעוּ אֶת־קוֹלְכֶם וְלֹא־יֵצֵא מִפִּיכֶם דָּבָר
The phrases You shall not shout, you shall not make your voice heard, and a word shall not go out from your mouth mean very similar things.
Joshua is using the term day to refer to a specific time.
6:11: Here, the word he refers to Joshua. It is implied that Joshua did not carry the Box of the Lord around Jericho himself, but rather, instructed the priests do it.
6:13: The author may be expressing a single idea by using two words connected with and. While the priests actually were walking and blowing on the shofars at the same time, the word walking might be describing in what way the priests were blowing, that is, continually.
6:15: The author is using the word dawn by association to mean the sun.
6:16: As in Joshua 6:5 and Joshua 6:10, the phrase the people refers to the Israelite soldiers.
6:17: To decide how to translate the term devoted here, in the next verse, and in verse 21, see the discussion in the Introduction to Joshua.
6:21: When he speaks of man and woman, and also when he speaks of young and old, the author is using two things to mean them and everything in between.
To decide how to translate this expression here and in its other occurrences, see the discussion in the Introduction to Joshua.
6:24: The phrase the house of the Lord is another name for the tent of meeting.
6:25: וַתֵּשֶׁב בְּקֶרֶב יִשְׂרָאֵל עַד הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה
Depending on when this account was written, the word she could refer to: (1) Rahab herself; (2) Rahab’s descendants.
The author is speaking of the Israelite people by association with the man Israel from whom they descended.
6:26: By With and with, Joshua does not mean that the man he is describing will work together with his oldest son to lay the foundations of Jericho and work together with his youngest son to set up its gates. Rather, he means that these sons will die at the beginning and ending of the rebuilding.
7:1: In this verse, the author is providing background information that will help readers understand what happens next in the story.

For emphasis, the author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. The idea is that one Israelite did something secret and deceptive that was a betrayal of the trust that the Lord had placed in all of the Israelites.
To decide how to translate the term devoted in its two instances here and throughout this chapter, see the discussion in the Introduction to Joshua.
Achan, Karmi, Zabdi, and Zerah are the names of men.
The author is using the nose of the Lord to mean his anger, by association with the way that a person who is angry breathes heavily through his nose.
The author is speaking as if the nose of the Lord, representing his anger, had actually burned. He means that his anger became very intense.
7:2: The author is describing the location of one place relative to another in the way that is characteristic of his culture. He means that if someone were traveling from Bethel to Beth Aven, he would be coming from the east.
7:3: As in Joshua 6:5 and several other places in chapter 6, the phrase the people refers to the Israelite soldiers.
7:4: See the Introduction to Joshua for a discussion of the phrase “to the face of.”
7:5: The word translated as the quarries could be: (1) a description of a geographic feature near the city of Ai; (2) the name of a place.
A quarry is a place from which people take stones to use for building things. Normally, quarries are large holes that go deep in the ground.
The expressions melted and became water mean similar things. The author is using them together for emphasis.
The author is speaking as if the hearts of the Israelite soldiers actually became water. This is another way of saying that the soldiers became afraid.
7:6: Joshua tore his garments as a symbolic act to show his grief and distress.
Joshua put dust on his head as a further symbolic act done to show grief.
7:7: This phrase expresses a single idea by using two verbs connected with and. The verb had been content tells in what way Joshua wishes the Israelites had stayed on the other side of the Jordan River.
7:8: Joshua is using the question form for emphasis.
Joshua is using a common expression to mean that the Israelite soldiers stopped fighting and ran away from the battle.
7:9: Joshua is speaking as if the Canaanite people groups would actually cut off the name of the Israelites from the earth, as if their name were a physical part of the earth. He is using their name to represent their reputation and the memory of them, he is using the phrase cut off to mean “bring to an end” or “cause to cease,” and he is using the earth to mean the people who live on the earth.
Joshua is using the question form for emphasis. He is using the Lord’s name to represent his reputation.
7:10: The Lord is not asking for information. He is using the question form to rebuke Joshua.
7:11: This phrase expresses a single idea by using two verbs connected with and. The verb transgressed tells in what way Israel has sinned.
7:13: While the Lord does want Joshua to get up from kneeling down with his face on the ground, he is probably using the expression Arise to tell him to take action.
7:16: The cultural context suggests that Joshua may have used lots (small, marked stones) in this process, expecting that the Lord would control which way they fell and thus guide the identification process.
7:17: The word Zerahite is the name of a clan made up of the descendants of the man named Zerah, who was the great-grandfather of Achan mentioned in Joshua 7:1.

The author is using the name Zabdi by association to mean his house or extended family, as 7:14 indicates. Zabdi was the grandfather of Achan, and Achan would have been included in his extended family.
7:19: Joshua is using the expression give glory to the Lord the God of Israel to encourage Achan to tell the truth and admit what he has done wrong. This will give glory to the Lord by vindicating his justice that led him to allow the people of Ai to defeat the Israelites.
7:20: Achan is using a common expression of his culture, like this and like this, to mean that he is about to provide exact details.
7:21: At that time, a shekel was a measure of weight.
7:22: The author is using the word behold to focus attention on what happens next in this story.
7:23: This could mean: (1) “where the Lord could see them.” The idea is not that the Lord did not know their location before; he told Joshua in Joshua 7:11 that an Israelite had stolen some of the devoted things and hidden them. Rather, the idea is that this was public evidence that the Israelites had found the wrongdoer and would punish him as the Lord had told them to; (2) “in front of the tent of meeting.” The phrase could be a description of where the Israelites poured … out the silver coins, coat, and gold wedge. The author would be using the name The Lord by association to mean the place where his presence was. But this would also indicate that these things were serving as conclusive evidence against Achan.
7:24: This phrase does not mean that Joshua also brought all Israel to the Valley of Achor when he brought Achan there. It means that Joshua and all Israel with him brought Achan and his family and possessions to the Valley of Achor.
The Hebrew word Achor is the name of a valley. As the next two verses explain, the word means “trouble,” and the Israelites gave that name to the valley on this occasion.
7:25: Joshua is using the question form to rebuke Achan.
וַיִּרְגְּמוּ אֹתוֹ כָל־יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶבֶן … וַיִּסְקְלוּ אֹתָם בָּאֲבָנִים
For emphasis, the author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root.
7:26: Here, the expression turned from means “stopped” or “ceased.”
8:1: The phrases Do not fear and do not be dismayed mean similar things. The Lord is using them together to emphasize that Joshua and the Israelite soldiers must not be afraid.
8:8: Joshua is using the term word by association to represent what the Lord has said by using words.
8:9: As the introduction to this chapter discusses, here and several other times in the following verses, the author describes the location of one place relative to another in the way that is characteristic of his culture.
8:10: See the Introduction to Joshua for a discussion of the phrase “to the face of.”
8:12: וַיִּקַּח כַּחֲמֵשֶׁת אֲלָפִים אִישׁ וַיָּשֶׂם אוֹתָם אֹרֵב

This statement seems to be a reminder of what Joshua did in Joshua 8:3–9. For a discussion of why Joshua 8:3 says that Joshua sent 30,000 men to lie in ambush while this verse says that he sent about 5,000 men, see the introduction to this chapter.
8:13: The author is speaking of the Israelite army as if it were a foot and the soldiers who hid west of Ai as its heel. He means that those soldiers were at the edge of the force.
8:14: The author does not say specifically what the king of Ai saw. This could mean: (1) that the king saw Joshua. The author has just said that Joshua went and spent the night in the valley near Ai, and the king may have seen him in the morning and concluded that this was the main force of the Israelite army and that he could attack and destroy it; (2) that the king saw that the Israelite army was north of the city. This could be a more general reference to the king seeing that the Israelites had set up their main camp to the north of the city.
This phrase expresses a single idea by using two words connected with and. The word hurried tells in what way the men of the city got up early.
As in Joshua 6:5, the term people refers to soldiers.
8:15: See the section discussing the word “struck” in the Introduction to Joshua and also see the section discussing the phrase “to the face of.”
8:16: In this context, the phrase the people refers to the men who were able to fight. It is clear from Joshua 8:24 that other people remained in the city.
8:17: Here, the term man refers specifically to the men who were able to fight. They left these two cities to pursue the Israelite army. Older men and those unable to fight because of some physical disability probably did not leave these cities.
The statement that the fighting men of Bethel also pursued the Israelites implicitly suggests that Bethel and Ai were allied cities.
8:18: This action was a literal sign to Joshua’s soldiers to attack Ai, as the next verse indicates, but it was probably also a symbolic indication that Ai was to be destroyed.
8:19: This phrase expresses a single idea by using two words connected with and. The word hurried tells in what way the soldiers from the ambush burned the city.
8:20: The author is using the term behold to focus attention on what happens next in this story.
וְלֹא־הָיָה בָהֶם יָדַיִם לָנוּס הֵנָּה וָהֵנָּה

Here, hand represents the capability of a person. This statement seems to introduce the action that the author describes in the rest of this verse and in the next two verses, in which the soldiers from Ai and Bethel become surrounded by the Israelite soldiers.
The author is speaking of two things in order to mean them and everything in between.
8:22: וַיִּהְיוּ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל בַּתָּוֶךְ אֵלֶּה מִזֶּה וְאֵלֶּה מִזֶּה

The author is using the term Israel by association to mean the Israelite army. It is not significant which instance of here refers to which body of Israelite soldiers, the one coming from the city or the one coming back from the wilderness.
8:24: The author is describing dying in battle by association with the word fallen, since soldiers who die in battle fall to the ground in their dying.
8:26: The author is expressing a positive meaning by using a negative word together with a term that is the opposite of the action he wishes to emphasize.
8:27: The author is using the term word to represent what the Lord commanded by using words.
8:31: The author is quoting the Lord’s words to Moses in Exodus 20:25 where the Lord uses the first part of a process to mean that entire process. Picking up an iron tool and holding it over a stone is the first step in using that tool to shape the stone.
8:33: As the introduction to this chapter discusses, the author is describing the location of one place relative to another in the way that is characteristic of his culture.
8:35: The author is making clear that on this occasion the assembly of Israel did not consist only of male representatives of tribes or clans or extended families, but that it also included women and children and sojourners.
9:1: The description that follows indicates that by the other side of the Jordan, the author means the side opposite to the one from which the Israelites approached the land of Canaan.
9:6: See the discussion of this phrase in the introduction to this chapter.
9:7: The Israelite leaders are using the question form for emphasis.
9:8: By saying We are your servants, the Gibeonites do not mean that they are willing to become slaves, such as they eventually do become in this episode. Rather, they are agreeing to let Joshua be their ruler. They mean implicitly that they will accept the terms he specifies, such as paying tribute.
9:9: Here, as in Joshua 7:9, the Lord’s name represents his reputation.
9:10: The word Ashtaroth is the name of the capital city of Bashan.
9:11: The Gibeonites and their leaders were using one part of a person, his hand, to represent all of him in the act of bringing something with them.
The people of Gibeon are speaking of the men’s journey by association with the road on which they would walk.
9:12: In this context, the Gibeonites are using the term behold to mean that they want the Israelites to look at their bread.
9:13: The Gibeonites are using the word behold here in the same way as in the previous verse.
9:14: This could mean: (1) that the Israelite leaders tasted the provisions of the Gibeonites to see whether they were old; (2) that they took some of these provisions out of the Gibeonites’ baggage to examine them.
The author is using the Lord’s mouth to represent the Lord himself in the act of guiding or giving counsel.
9:16: וַיִּשְׁמְעוּ כִּי־קְרֹבִים הֵם אֵלָיו וּבְקִרְבּוֹ הֵם יֹשְׁבִים

The phrases they were near to them and they were dwelling among them mean basically the same thing. The author says the same thing twice, in slightly different ways, to emphasize that the Gibeonites lived close to the Israelites.
9:17: Kephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath Jearim are the names of towns that were subject to the king of the city of Gibeon.
9:20: The leaders mean implicitly that they do not want the wrath of the Lord to be upon them, that is, they do not want the Lord to be angry with them and punish them for breaking their oath.
9:25: Here, the hand represents the power or control that a person has over someone or something.
The terms good and right mean similar things. The author is using the two terms together for emphasis.
9:26: The author is using one part of the sons of Israel, their hand, to represent all of them in the potential act of killing the Gibeonites.
10:1: See the discussion of the term devoted in the introduction to this chapter.
10:5: The author is using the term camps by association to mean the armies that stayed in camps during military campaigns.
